summary.none: Nothing we checked crossed its threshold. That means we found no problem in what we measured — not that the site is necessarily fast.

autoload-oversized.title: Autoloaded options are too large
autoload-oversized.why: Every autoloaded row in the options table is read and unserialized on every request — not just pages, but admin-ajax, REST and cron too. That cost is paid on every visit, every time.

autoload-orphans.title: Orphaned autoload rows
autoload-orphans.why: Plugins usually leave their options behind when they are deleted. Those rows are read on every request forever, without any code using them.

no-object-cache.title: No external object cache
no-object-cache.why: Without Redis or Memcached, every option and query result cached in memory is lost at the end of the request, and the next request starts from zero.

n-plus-one.title: One query runs over and over
n-plus-one.why: When the same query shape runs dozens of times on one page, it almost always means code inside a loop is hitting the database once per item. This is the pattern that makes a page slower and slower as content grows.

heavy-plugin.title: One plugin takes most of the database time
heavy-plugin.why: When one plugin owns the dominant share of a page's query time, that is the right place to start — not generic speed settings.

slow-query.title: Slow query
slow-query.why: A single query that takes more than 50 ms on its own usually lacks an index or scans a table that has grown very large.

expired-transients.title: Expired transients have piled up
expired-transients.why: Without an external object cache, expired transients stay in the options table. A bigger table means slower autoload reads.

revision-bloat.title: A large pile of post revisions
revision-bloat.why: Every edit creates a row in the posts table. Hundreds of thousands of revision rows do not slow pages themselves, but they make every query on posts and every backup heavier.

cron-backlog.title: Scheduled tasks are falling behind
cron-backlog.why: WordPress runs cron on visitor requests. When the queue falls behind, the next visitor pays for that work — and they are the one whose page loads slowly.

old-php.title: PHP version is outdated
old-php.why: Every major PHP release since 7 has made the same code run noticeably faster. This is the cheapest improvement available.

no-opcache.title: OPcache is off
no-opcache.why: Without OPcache, PHP recompiles every file on every request. Turning it on does not change how the site behaves.

page-served-from-cache.title: This page never reached PHP
page-served-from-cache.why: A cache layer served the page as static output. For visitors, that is the best possible case.

autoloadOversized.intro: Look at the largest ones and do one of these three things for each:
autoloadOversized.removed: 1) If it belongs to a plugin that is no longer installed, delete the row.
autoloadOversized.active: 2) If it belongs to an active plugin, you usually want to set its autoload to no — not delete it.
autoloadOversized.cache: 3) If it is a cache, it is better moved to a transient or the object cache — that is a change the plugin itself has to make.
autoloadOversized.orphans_one: {count} row has no identifiable owner; such rows are usually left over from deleted plugins and are the safest to remove.
autoloadOversized.orphans_other: {count} rows have no identifiable owner; these are usually left over from deleted plugins and are the safest to remove.

autoloadOrphans.total: {count} large rows with no known owner, {size} in total.
autoloadOrphans.backup: Back up the database before deleting anything — this tool can do that for you.
autoloadOrphans.unsure: If you are not sure what a row belongs to, set its autoload to no instead of deleting it: the speed effect is the same and it is reversible.

noObjectCache.install: If your host offers Redis, install and activate the Redis Object Cache plugin.
noObjectCache.needsRedis: This requires a Redis service on the host — without it, the plugin does nothing.
noObjectCache.shared: It is usually unavailable on shared hosting; in that case, ignore this item.

nPlusOne.worst: Worst case: one query shape ran {count} times, {ms} ms in total.
nPlusOne.noSource: The source could not be identified.
nPlusOne.owner: The plugin or theme itself has to fix this — usually with one batched query instead of a query inside a loop.
nPlusOne.thirdParty: If it is a third-party plugin, check for a newer version or report it to the developer.

heavyPlugin.share: {source} alone takes {share}% of this page's query time ({queries} queries, {ms} ms).
heavyPlugin.settings: Start with that plugin's own settings: many plugins have an option to limit their work to the pages that need it.
heavyPlugin.conflict: With “Conflict check” you can see how the page loads without this plugin.

slowQuery.postmeta: If it runs on postmeta, it is usually a meta_query without a suitable index.
slowQuery.cleanup: Cleaning up orphaned meta and optimizing tables is sometimes enough; otherwise the code that owns the query has to be fixed.

expiredTransients.safe: Removing them is safe: they have expired, so no code relies on them any more, and they are rebuilt if needed.

revisionBloat.limit: To stop them growing back, set WP_POST_REVISIONS in wp-config.php, for example to 5.
revisionBloat.irreversible: Deleting old revisions cannot be undone — the edit history is lost. Back up first.
revisionBloat.orphanMeta: There are also {count} orphaned meta rows not attached to any post.

cronBacklog.overdue: {count} tasks have not run for more than an hour.
cronBacklog.disabled: DISABLE_WP_CRON is on, so a real cron job should be configured on the server. It apparently is not, or it is not working.
cronBacklog.enable: Best fix: turn on DISABLE_WP_CRON and add a host cron job that calls wp-cron.php every 5 minutes.
cronBacklog.relief: That takes the heavy work off your visitors.

oldPhp.upgrade: Upgrading to 8.2 or later is done from the hosting control panel.
oldPhp.backup: Back up before upgrading and check the main pages afterwards: very old plugins may throw errors.

noOpcache.enable: Turn on opcache.enable in the host's PHP settings.
noOpcache.askHost: If you do not have access, ask your host — it is a standard setting with no risk.

pageCached.bypass: To see this page's real queries, you need to bypass the cache for that URL temporarily.
